case_study_insert.main_stem: Cedar Grove Furniture (CGF) is a partnership in the furniture manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2013 by the cabinet maker Ingrid Solberg, it makes solid-wood cabinets for independent retailers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. CGF plans to invest $560,000 in CNC cutting machinery, financed by $360,000 of hire purchase and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $165,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.00, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. CGF is battling timber waste of 8.5% and a shortage of CNC-trained cabinet makers that threatens delivery targets to independent retailers across the country.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The assembly shop finished 9,600 units last quarter at a defect rate of 3.3%, down from 5.1% a year ago. Customer complaints about finish fell from 44 to 19 per month and timber waste was 8.5% of material input. Average delivery time is 7.4 days. A survey of 320 homeowners found 58% prefer FSC-certified timber and 46% would pay $12 more per item. A skills check shows 11 of 35 cabinet makers need CNC training; external CNC courses cost $1,100 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Cedar Grove Furniture as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, making hire-purchase finance dearer. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 5.5% from $13.00 to $13.72 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale timber and wood-panel input costs rose 8.7% year-on-year, while new-build furniture demand grew 2.4%.

questions.question_text: CGF is financing $360,000 of its $560,000 CNC machinery through hire purchase. Explain two advantages for CGF of hire purchase over borrowing the full amount from a bank.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $360,000 cost into manageable regular payments, so CGF does not need a large lump sum and can keep cash for the $200,000 retained-profit contribution and daily operations. With fixed costs of $165,000 a year already to meet, smoother payments protect the $5.50 contribution on each of the 40,000 units and make the $560,000 machinery affordable for a partnership of 35.

Point 2: The machinery itself serves as security for the hire-purchase agreement, so CGF may find finance easier to obtain than an unsecured bank loan of the same size, and ownership passes once payments finish. This lets Ingrid Solberg install the CNC machines quickly to cut the 8.5% timber waste, which raises efficiency without handing a bank a claim over the whole business.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of hire purchase identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to CGF, its $560,000 machinery and its costs.

questions.question_text: CGF wants to grow sales of its solid-wood cabinets. Consider selling through independent retailers, an own e-commerce website, or a factory outlet. Which should CGF choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Independent retailers: CGF already supplies independent retailers, so deepening this channel uses existing relationships and the 58% of 320 homeowners who prefer FSC-certified timber can be reached through shops that can display the finish of the 9,600 units made last quarter. Retailers add a margin and may demand display stock, which ties up cash, and CGF has only 35 staff to service many accounts. Retail partners also control the customer relationship and the 7.4-day delivery promise.

Own e-commerce website: A website lets CGF show every cabinet, take orders directly and keep the full $13.00 selling price rather than sharing a retailer's margin; the 46% of homeowners who would pay $12 more can be targeted with FSC-certified storytelling. Set-up and digital marketing cost money and CGF has no online-sales experience, while bulky cabinets create delivery and returns problems that could strain the 7.4-day lead time.

Factory outlet: A shop at the workshop sells Seconds and excess stock directly, useful for reducing the 8.5% timber waste and the 3.3% defect rate by recovering some value from imperfect units. It is limited by location, attracts bargain hunters rather than buyers willing to pay a $12 premium, and needs staff to run it when 11 cabinet makers already need CNC training.

Recommendation: CGF should choose the own e-commerce website. It captures the full price, reaches the 58%/46% research segments nationally and supports the $5.50 contribution needed to justify the $560,000 CNC investment. Independent retailers are rejected because their margin and control reduce that contribution, and the factory outlet is rejected as a low-price channel that cannot build the premium brand CGF needs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the distribution channels with minimal application to CGF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two channels in CGF's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discussion of all three channels with a justified recommendation explaining why retailers and the factory outlet are rejected.

questions.question_text: CGF has a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership, timber waste of 8.5% and 11 cabinet makers needing CNC training. Explain two benefits for CGF of introducing job rotation.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation moves cabinet makers between cutting, assembly and finishing, so staff learn several stages and understand how the 8.5% timber waste arises. With a flat structure and laissez-faire leadership, workers can suggest better cutting patterns themselves, reducing waste and lowering the 3.3% defect rate without waiting for Ingrid Solberg to issue instructions.

Point 2: Rotation spreads the 11 workers who need CNC training across different machines, building a more flexible team of 35 that can cover absences and keep the 40,000-unit output on schedule. Variety also reduces boredom and improves motivation, which helps retain skilled staff and protects the $560,000 CNC investment and the $5.50 contribution per unit.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of job rotation identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CGF's waste, training needs and output.

questions.question_text: Eleven of CGF's 35 cabinet makers need CNC skills. Consider recruiting an experienced CNC operator externally or retraining an existing supervisor. Which should CGF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External recruitment: Hiring a qualified CNC operator brings proven skills immediately, so the $560,000 machines can run at capacity and the 8.5% timber waste can be tackled from day one. The newcomer can coach others, which suits the flat structure. The costs are advertising, selection and a likely higher salary, and an outside hire may not fit the team or understand CGF's solid-wood products, while a hire-purchase commitment of $360,000 already weighs on cash.

Retraining an existing supervisor: A supervisor who knows the 9,600-unit assembly routine and the 3.3% finish complaints can learn CNC programming and then train the 11 others, which is cheaper than recruitment and builds loyalty. External CNC courses cost $1,100 per person; even training several staff is small beside $560,000. The drawback is the learning time before the supervisor can teach others, during which output may dip and the 7.4-day delivery promise could be at risk.

Decision: CGF should retrain the existing supervisor. The firm's problem is a lack of CNC skills across 11 of 35 staff, and a supervisor who understands CGF's products can diffuse those skills to the whole team, which external recruitment alone would not do. Recruitment is rejected because a higher salary and an unknown fit add cost and risk on top of $360,000 of hire purchase; the short learning dip can be managed by phasing the 40,000-unit schedule. Once the supervisor is certified, CGF can send the other 11 on the $1,100 courses.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of recruitment and retraining with limited application to CGF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in CGF's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision covering cost, speed and skill transfer.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how the management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $165,000 ÷ ($13.00 − $7.50) = $165,000 ÷ $5.50 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.00 − $7.50 = $5.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CGF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with 40,000 units produced: the margin of safety is 10,000 units, showing how far sales can fall before the $165,000 fixed costs are not covered.
2. Use the $5.50 contribution to test the $12 premium that 46% of homeowners would pay; adding it to the $13.00 price would lift contribution sharply, which managers can balance against a possible fall in volume.
3. Use unit cost of $11.63 ($165,000 ÷ 40,000 = $4.13 plus $7.50 variable cost) to monitor the 8.5% timber waste and set a target for cutting it.
4. Use labour productivity of about 1,143 units per worker (40,000 ÷ 35) to judge whether the 11 CNC trainees can be trained without disrupting the 7.4-day delivery promise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 10,000-unit margin of safety; $12 premium pricing; unit cost $11.63 to cut 8.5% timber waste; labour productivity about 1,143 units per worker for training plans.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CGF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CGF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.47 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.77 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.64 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $110,000 inventories + $70,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $225,000; 2025 current assets = $150,000 + $95,000 + $20,000 = $265,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $225,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.50; the 2025 comparison is $265,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.47. The stock-excluding measure for 2024 is ($225,000 − $110,000) ÷ $150,000 = $115,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.77; for 2025 it is ($265,000 − $150,000) ÷ $180,000 = $115,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.64.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. Current assets rose from $225,000 to $265,000, but current liabilities grew faster, from $150,000 to $180,000, so the 2024 figure of 1.50 slipped to 1.47 in 2025. More seriously, the stock-excluding measure fell from 0.77 to 0.64 because cash dropped from $45,000 to $20,000 while inventories climbed from $110,000 to $150,000 and receivables from $70,000 to $95,000. That means CGF is increasingly relying on selling timber stock to meet bills, which is risky while it has a $360,000 hire-purchase commitment and $560,000 of new machinery. The 8.5% timber waste makes the growing inventory especially worrying: some stock may be slow to turn into cash. Still-rising receivables also suggest independent retailers are paying more slowly.

Conclusion: CGF's financial position has not improved; it has worsened. Both measures fell (1.50 to 1.47 and 0.77 to 0.64), and the decline in the stock-excluding position shows the problem is not just inventory. CGF should cut the 8.5% waste, chase the $95,000 of receivables and rebuild cash before taking on more hire purchase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on whether financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CGF of using FSC-certified timber in its cabinets.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey shows 58% of 320 homeowners prefer FSC-certified timber and 46% would pay $12 more per item, so CGF can charge a premium above its $13.00 selling price and protect the $5.50 contribution per unit even with an 8.7% rise in timber costs. It also differentiates CGF from rivals when selling through independent retailers and supports the $560,000 CNC investment.

Disadvantage: Certified timber may cost more than standard wood, raising the $7.50 variable cost per unit and squeezing the $5.50 contribution. If certified supply is short, the 8.5% timber waste and 7.4-day delivery promise could worsen, and the 3.3% defect rate on finish may rise if substitute woods behave differently in the new CNC machines.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CGF's research, costs and machinery.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in timber and wood-panel costs will affect CGF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): CGF has $360,000 of hire purchase rather than a bank loan, but dearer credit still matters: a 0.75% rise applied illustratively to $360,000 is $2,700 a year (0.0075 × $360,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $165,000 a year, and the impact depends on the agreement's terms, which the insert does not give, so no larger figure should be invented. The main effect is on the cost of any future finance.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.72 an hour): Some of the workforce of 35 is likely hourly-paid, so wage costs rise. The insert states no hours worked or pay by role, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 40,000 units ÷ 35 workers = about 1,143 units per worker. If the $560,000 CNC machines raise output per worker, the wage rise is affordable; if the 11 untrained cabinet makers and 8.5% timber waste hold output back, unit labour cost rises and the $5.50 contribution shrinks.

Timber and wood-panel costs (8.7%): These feed the $7.50 variable cost per unit, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a labelled bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 8.7%, that is 8.7% × $7.50 = about $0.65 per unit; across 40,000 units that is roughly $26,000 a year (40,000 × $0.65). The 46% of homeowners who would pay $12 more offer pricing room, but new-build furniture demand grew only 2.4%, so a full price rise may lose orders.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in timber costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 40,000 cabinets and directly erodes the $5.50 contribution supporting the $560,000 machinery; the interest effect is at most about $2,700 on the hire purchase, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity gains from the CNC machines.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CGF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CGF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
